# Dependence and the Anna Karenina principle

As the great novelist Leo Tolstoy wrote in his 1878 novel Anna Karenina:

> "Все счастливые семьи похожи друг на друга, каждая несчастливая семья несчастлива по-своему."

Meaning: all happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way. But it sounds much better in Russian.

In probability, as in life, all happy families of independent variables are alike; each unhappy family of dependent variables is unhappy, or dependent, in its own way.

If my grandmother were to sample an absolutely random group of 20 different kids and record their shoe size (and age), we would have a happy family of independent variables, and we could have multiplied their probability densities, got our likelihood and maximized it to get our parameters.

Too fast? Let's take it slower.

If my grandmother were to sample an absolutely random group of 20 different kids and record their shoe size (and age), she could go with the simple global model:

$$
\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_j} = \text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{slope}_{\text{global}} \times \text{age} + \text{error}_{\text{kid}_j}
$$

where $\text{intercept}_{\text{global}}$ and $\text{slope}_{\text{global}}$ are the global, fixed, intercept and slope parameters, and $\text{error}_{\text{kid}_j}$ is the random error term coming from a $\mathcal{N}(0, \text{var}_{\text{error}})$ distribution, and each error term is independent of the other error terms.

Now here's a subtle point:

- The only random variable in the right-hand side of the model would be the error term $\text{error}_{\text{kid}_j}$.
- The age of each kid $j$ would be a known, fixed value.
- The $\text{intercept}_{\text{global}}$ and $\text{slope}_{\text{global}}$ would be unknown, but also fixed. Not random variables.
- So this entire term: $\{\text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{slope}_{\text{global}} \times \text{age}\}$ would be a constant. You can call it $c$.

What would this mean for kid $j$'s $\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_j}$?

Kid $j$'s shoe size would be a random variable that is normally distributed with a mean of $\{\text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{slope}_{\text{global}} \times \text{age}\}$ and a variance of $\text{var}_{\text{error}}$, or:

$$\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_j} \sim \mathcal{N}(\text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{slope}_{\text{global}} \times \text{age}, \text{var}_{\text{error}})$$

This actually needs proof, but we'll skip it for now. All I'm saying is that if we have a random variable $X$ (the error term) with a $\mathcal{N}(0, \text{var})$ distribution --- you know, that bell curve shape --- and we add to it a constant $c$ (intercept + slope x age), then the distribution of $X + c$ is $\mathcal{N}(c, \text{var})$ --- the same bell curve shape, but shifted by $c$.

This leads us to the next subtle point:

This distribution of kid $j$'s shoe size is **only** a function of kid $j$ --- their age which is given, and a personal random error term, which is independent of the other kids' error terms. A kid $j$'s shoe size isn't dependent on the other kids --- their shoe sizes, ages or error terms. That is why I say the kids' shoe sizes would be independent, just like the heights of random individuals from the previous [post](./08_likelihood.qmd), a happy family.

The likelihood would be the product of the probability densities of each kid's shoe size:

$$
\begin{align}
Likelihood &= f(\text{the data we observed}) \\
&= f(\text{Kid 1's shoe size is 25.4}, \text{Kid 2's shoe size is 19.9}, \dots) \\
&= f(\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_1} = 25.4, \text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_2} = 19.9, \dots, \text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_{20}} = 33.2) \\
&= f(\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_1} = 25.4) \times f(\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_2} = 19.9) \times \cdots \times f(\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_{20}} = 33.2)
\end{align}
$$

And each of those $f(\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_j} = S)$ is a normal probability density term --- a daunting yet simple formula --- a function of the kid's age which is given, the global intercept and slope, and the variance of the error term --- three unknown parameters. So we would maximize the likelihood (or minimize the negative likelihood, you know, a loss function) to get the best values for these three parameters, which amounts, by the way, to a simple formula in this case.

Wait! Why am I so obsessed with factorizing the likelihood into a product of probability densities? What makes this independent model a "happy family"?

I'll tell you why, but you need to promise you won't flip --- a *product* of quantities can easily be made into a *sum* of quantities, by taking the logarithm :open_mouth:.^[A logarithm is just a function, any calculator has it, chill.] This is called the *log-likelihood*. Put a minus sign in front and it is the *negative* log-likelihood.

And a sum is even easier to handle, as we'll see later on.

But that's not all! Remember the [sum of squares](./03_learning.qmd) loss function we wanted to minimize?

$$
\text{Sum of squares} = (\text{real shoe size}_{\text{kid}_1} - \text{predicted shoe size}_{\text{kid}_1})^2 + \dots + (\text{real shoe size}_{\text{kid}_{20}} - \text{predicted shoe size}_{\text{kid}_{20}})^2
$$

Then, in this case of normal probability densities, forgetting about the $\text{var}_{\text{error}}$ term for a moment, the sum of squares is just the negative log-likelihood!^[Well, not exactly, it is *proportional* to the negative log-likelihood, that's why we write $\propto$ instead of $=$.] :scream: :scream: :scream:

$$
\text{Sum of squares} \propto -\log(Likelihood)
$$

So independence is a happy family: maximizing the likelihood is minimizing the sum of squares. Independence is easy.

Dependence is hard.

What would a dependent model look like?

Suppose the 20 different kids were sampled in sequence:

$$\{(\text{age}, \text{shoe size})_{(1)}, (\text{age}, \text{shoe size})_{(2)}, \dots, (\text{age}, \text{shoe size})_{(20)}\}$$

The first kid's shoe size would be modeled as:

$$
\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_{(1)}} = \text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{slope}_{\text{global}} \times \text{age} + \text{error}_{\text{kid}_{(1)}}
$$

But then, unbeknownst to my grandmother, some hidden mechanism would be at play, and the shoe size of each kid starting with the second kid ($j=2$) would be dependent on the shoe size of the previous kid ($j-1$), like so:

$$
\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_{(j)}} = \text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{slope}_{\text{global}} \times \text{age} + \text{error}_{\text{kid}_{(j)}} + 0.1 \times \text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_{(j - 1)}}
$$

That is a dependent model.

The distribution of each kid's shoe size --- a.k.a. the *marginal* distribution --- is still a normal distribution^[Again, this needs proof, but we'll skip it for now.]. We can still write:

$$
\begin{align}
Likelihood &= f(\text{the data we observed}) \\
&= f(\text{Kid 1's shoe size is 25.4}, \text{Kid 2's shoe size is 19.9}, \dots) \\
&= f(\text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_1} = 25.4, \text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_2} = 19.9, \dots, \text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_{20}} = 33.2) 
\end{align}
$$

But now, we cannot simply *factorize* the likelihood into the product of the probability densities of each kid's shoe size. Why? Because the shoe size of each kid is dependent on the shoe size of the previous kid. So we need to somehow take into account the dependency structure of the data.^[In this specific case, we *can* actually factorize the likelihood into a product of *conditional* probability densities, but that's a story for another time.]

That's just one unhappy family. The Anna Karenina principle tells us that there are many more.

Why invent? We have our own unhappy family!

Recall, each kid's shoe size is repeatedly measured in different ages. Each kid $j$ has their own pair of $(\text{i-diff}_{\text{kid}_j}, \text{s-diff}_{\text{kid}_j})$ intercept and slope differences from the global intercept and slope, which are samples of normal random variables, and not treated as fixed parameters. The model is then:

$$ \text{shoe size}_{\text{global}} = \text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{slope}_{\text{global}} \times \text{age} $$
$$ \text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_1} = (\text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{i-diff}_{\text{kid}_1}) + (\text{slope}_{\text{global}} + \text{s-diff}_{\text{kid}_1}) \times \text{age} + \text{error}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_1} $$
$$ \text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_2} = (\text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{i-diff}_{\text{kid}_2}) + (\text{slope}_{\text{global}} + \text{s-diff}_{\text{kid}_2}) \times \text{age} + \text{error}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_2} $$
$$\vdots$$

$$ \text{shoe size}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_{10}} = (\text{intercept}_{\text{global}} + \text{i-diff}_{\text{kid}_{10}}) + (\text{slope}_{\text{global}} + \text{s-diff}_{\text{kid}_{10}}) \times \text{age} + \text{error}_{\text{age}, \text{kid}_{10}} $$

If we knew the $(\text{i-diff}_{\text{kid}_j}, \text{s-diff}_{\text{kid}_j})$ random differences for each kid, we would have a happy family. Each observation of a kid's shoe size at any age would be independent of the other observations of the same kid's shoe size at any other age, or any other kid's shoe size at any other age. But we don't know them, and they are not fixed parameters. They are random variables, and we need to somehow take them into account.

In this unhappy family, we can still show that marginally each kid's shoe size at any age is normally distributed. We can still write the likelihood.^[We'd either need linear algebra or some freakishly complex term.] But we cannot factorize it into the product of 20 probability densities of each kid's shoe size at any age.^[We *can* factorize it into a product of 10 *multivariate* normal probability densities, but that's so out of scope.] Why? Because within each kid, the shoe sizes are not independent of each other. Once a kid "sampled" their $(\text{i-diff}_{\text{kid}_j}, \text{s-diff}_{\text{kid}_j})$ random differences, they are stuck with them their whole life (remember [Freud](./06_rvs_in_a_model.qmd)?) and they are shared with every age.

So remember: no independence $\rightarrow$ no factorization of likelihood into a product of 20 measurements $\rightarrow$ no sum of simple 20 quantities when we take the log $\rightarrow$ no sum of squares for us :cry:
